93	
94	Introduction
95	Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is a common injury in multi-directional field
96	sports (Moses et al., 2012). Surgical reconstruction of the ACL with either a bone-patellar
97	tendon-bone (BPTB) or hamstring (semitendinosus/gracilis) tendon (HT) autograft is
98	the most commonly selected treatment for athletes who wish to return to sport (RTS)
99	(Mihelic et al., 2011; Evans et al., 2014; Pinczewski et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2015). Following
100	ACLR, inter-limb deficits in neuromuscular activation, strength and power metrics are
101	evident as a result of the injury sustained and of graft harvesting (Myer et al., 2006;
102	
103	CONTACT Jill A. E. Costley          jillcostley@sportssurgeryclinic.com
104	© 2021 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
105	 2      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.
106	
107	
108	Palmieri-Smith et al., 2008; Xergia et al., 2011). Appropriate post-operative rehabilitation
109	to address functional inter-limb asymmetries is paramount for improving performance
110	capabilities and reducing re-injury rates (Buckthorpe, 2019; Grindem et al., 2016).
111	Successful rehabilitation also reduces the risk of further damage to chondral and menis­
112	cal structures and the onset of associated co-morbidities such as post-traumatic knee
113	osteoarthritis (Øiestad et al., 2015).
114	   A widely evaluated parameter of lower-limb function post-ACLR is knee extensor/
115	flexor muscle strength, assessed using isokinetic dynamometry (IKD) (Grindem et al.,
116	2016; Undheim et al., 2015). Although inter-limb strength symmetry is associated with
117	a lower risk of re-injury following ACLR (Grindem et al., 2016), asymmetries in tempo­
118	rally related metrics (rate of force development, impulse, etc.) frequently prevail beyond
119	the attainment of a symmetrical strength profile, even after RTS (Menzel et al., 2013;
120	Jordan et al., 2020). Pre-RTS assessment of neuromuscular ’readiness‘ should, therefore,
121	also consider the demands of the sport being returned to (Jordan et al., 2015). In multi-
122	directional field sports, jumping and landing motions are ubiquitous multi-joint actions
123	and are often characterised by concentric and eccentric demands (Lorenz, 2016; Miles
124	et al., 2019). Additionally, high eccentric loading upon initial ground contact (<50 ms)
125	during rapid deceleration is a known mechanism of non-contact ACL rupture
126	(Krosshaug et al., 2007). For such reasons, the double leg counter-movement jump
127	(CMJ) is often of interest in RTS assessment (Menzel et al., 2013; Jordan et al., 2020;
128	Jordan et al., 2015). In particular, the evaluation of phase-specific CMJ impulses,
129	obtained from the integration of the force-time profile, has enabled the quantification
130	and characterisation of asymmetry of distinct components of a single movement
131	(Baumgart et al., 2017; Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019).
132	   Vertical ground reaction force (GRF) impulse asymmetry has been identified as
133	a surrogate marker of knee kinetic deficits (moments and work) (Dai et al., 2014) associated
134	with heightened ACL re-injury risk (Paterno et al., 2010). Although CMJ concentric phase
135	symmetry has been found to improve with time after surgery (Read et al., 2020), eccentric
136	properties have displayed persistent deficits (Dai et al., 2020; Miles et al., 2019; Read et al.,
137	2020), especially following BPTB-ACLR (Miles et al., 2019), and slower recovery (Read
138	et al., 2020). However, recent evidence suggests that rates of recovery may be influenced by
139	graft type. For example, Cristiani et al. (2020) reported that inferior extensor strength
140	symmetry of BPTB-ACLR, relative to HT-ACLR, required up to 24 months post-
141	operatively to be addressed. Heightened functional performance asymmetries within
142	BPTB individuals, as assessed by single leg hop distance (SLHD), required only 6 months
143	post-ACLR (Cristiani et al., 2020). Yet, the SLHD test lacks the sensitivity to detect altered
144	technical execution (Cormie et al., 2009; King et al., 2019; Kotsifaki et al., 2019) and its
145	ability to predict successful outcomes following ACLR has been questioned (Davies et al.,
146	2020). Due to the common eccentric mechanism of ACL injury (Krosshaug et al., 2007), the
147	enduring deficits in eccentric qualities reported around the time of RTS (Grindem et al.,
148	2016; Miles et al., 2019; Read et al., 2020) may be of greater concern. Eccentric deficits have
149	been associated with an increased re-injury risk and may contribute to the high rates of
150	contralateral injury exhibited in ACLR populations by encouraging preferential use of the
151	contralateral limb (Miles et al., 2019; Paterno et al., 2010). In addition, only a weak
152	relationship has been observed between knee isokinetic strength inter-limb asymmetry
153	and CMJ impulse asymmetry 9 months post-ACLR (Miles et al., 2019), a time often
154	                                                                     SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        3
155	
156	
157	associated with RTS (Grindem et al., 2016). Thus, specific consideration of eccentric deficits
158	may be crucial when determining an athlete’s readiness to RTS; especially within the BPTB-
159	ACLR population who are reported to display the largest CMJ eccentric deficits, 9 months
160	post-surgery (Miles et al., 2019).
161	   Later-stage rehabilitation prior to RTS offers a valuable opportunity to optimise clinically-
162	related ACLR outcome measures in preparation for the on-field demands of play
163	(Buckthorpe, 2019; Grindem et al., 2016; Myer et al., 2006). Understanding the progression
164	of symmetry within key parameters of rehabilitation during this stage may allow persistent
165	asymmetries to be targeted more precisely, thereby increasing specificity of later-stage
166	rehabilitative protocols and RTS criteria. Thus, the aims of this study were two-fold: (1)
167	investigate the presence of systematic changes in CMJ phase-specific impulse and isokinetic
168	strength asymmetries between 6 and 9 months post-ACLR and whether they are affected by
169	graft type; and (2) examine the extent to which individual changes in impulse asymmetry can
170	be explained by changes in strength asymmetry. To assist with interpretations, we further
171	evaluated absolute values in all assessed strength and impulse variables of the independent
172	ACLR- and uninvolved-limb to investigate how observed changes in symmetry arose. It was
173	hypothesised that asymmetries in strength and phase-specific impulse would reduce from 6
174	to 9 months post-ACLR and that the magnitude of the reduction would not be modulated by
175	graft type. We expected that only weak relationships would be found between the progression
176	of strength asymmetries and the progression of CMJ impulse asymmetries, and that this
177	relationship would be strongest for the concentric phase of the jump.
178	
179	
180	Methods
181	Participants
182	Forty-four 18–35-year-old amateur male multidirectional field sport athletes undergoing
183	primary ACLR surgery at the Sports Surgery Clinic, Dublin, participated in this study.
184	Power analysis (G*Power, version 3.1.9.2, Universität Düsseldorf), recruitment proce­
185	dure, cohort demographics and anthropometric characteristics were as documented
186	previously (Miles et al., 2019). Participants had stated an intention to return to multi-
187	directional field sport and had undergone ACLR using either a hamstrings tendon (HT;
188	semitendinosus and gracilis; n = 22; age 26.1 ± 4.4 years, height 179.4 ± 6.1 cm, body mass
189	79.8 ± 9.4 kg) or BPTB (n = 22; age 23.4 ± 4.4 years, height 181.8 ± 6.4 cm, body mass
190	85.2 ± 11.5 kg) autologous ipsilateral graft. Those with previous ACLR, multiple con­
191	current ligament reconstructions or without an intention to return to multi-directional
192	field sports were excluded. Participants were predominantly involved in Gaelic football
193	(39%), hurling (23%), soccer (32%) and rugby (16%). Following ACLR, athletes com­
194	pleted two testing sessions: the first session at 5–7 months post-surgery (’6-month test’)
195	and the following at 8–10 months post-surgery (’9-month test’). Mean and standard
196	deviation (SD) time from surgery to the 6-month test was 6.2 ± 0.4 months (BPTB
197	6.4 ± 0.4, HT 6.1 ± 0.2) and to the 9-month test was 9.3 ± 0.4 months (BPTB 9.4 ± 0.4, HT
198	9.1 ± 0.3). At the 6- and 9-month testing session, respectively, the number of participants
199	that had returned to any level of sport was two and 22, while those who had returned to
200	their pre-injury level of sport was 0 and 12. The study was approved by the hospital’s
201	 4      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.
202	
203	
204	research ethics committee and informed written consent was obtained from participants
205	before testing. All testing procedures were as reported in Miles et al. (2019).
206	
207	
208	Testing procedures
209	Counter-movement jump performance
210	An identical protocol was used in the testing sessions 6 months and 9 months post-
211	ACLR, with each session beginning with the measurement of height and body mass.
212	A standardised warm-up consisting of a two-minute submaximal run at a self-
213	determined pace and five unloaded squats was subsequently performed and followed
214	by two maximal familiarisation CMJs. Participants were instructed to jump for maximal
215	height with lower limbs extended while airborne and hands placed on the iliac crests.
216	Three maximal CMJs were then performed on two force platforms (BP400600; AMTI,
217	Massachusetts, USA; 400 × 600 mm) with bilateral vertical ground reaction forces
218	(vGRF) recorded at 1000 Hz. Participants then completed a clinical assessment protocol
219	comprising additional jumps and change of direction manoeuvres.
220	
221	Concentric knee extensor and flexor strength
222	After laboratory testing, participants undertook a standardised, seated, IKD (Cybex
223	Humac NORM, CSMI) testing protocol to assess concentric knee flexor and extensor
224	strength (Undheim et al., 2015). The uninjured limb was tested first. For each limb, the
225	protocol consisted of three sets of five repetitions (60°/s) interspersed with 60 s rest: one
226	submaximal warm-up set followed by two maximal-effort sets with verbal encourage­
227	ment provided throughout. Concentric knee extensor and flexor peak torque was eval­
228	uated through 100° of range from 0° extension and sampled at 100 Hz. Finally, subjective
229	knee function was evaluated via the International Knee Documentation Committee
230	(IKDC) questionnaire (Irrgang et al., 2001).
231	
232	
233	Data processing
234	The impulse–momentum relationship was used to calculate vertical velocity of the centre of
235	mass (COM) at the instant of CMJ take-off (Linthorne, 2001), enabling the determination
236	of peak CMJ height. Three key phases of the CMJ were then identified using COM vertical
237	velocity: eccentric deceleration from maximal downwards velocity to zero velocity, con­
238	centric from zero velocity to take-off, and landing from landing to zero velocity
239	(Appendix 1) (Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019). The instants of take-off and landing
240	were identified using a vGRF threshold of 10 N. For each phase, limb-specific impulses were
241	derived by integration of force–time curves with extraction of impulse parameters facili­
242	tated by a custom MATLAB script (version 2015a, Mathworks Inc, Massachusetts, USA).
243	The mean of the three trials was used for all analysis.
244	   For evaluation of knee extension-flexion strength, a gravity correction was first
245	applied to IKD outputs. Peak knee extension and flexion torques were then obtained
246	from the maximal-effort set with the largest maximum knee extension torque and
247	repetition peak torque coefficient of <0.1. Both GRF impulses and isokinetic torques
248	were divided by body mass prior to further analysis.
249	                                                                    SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        5
250	
251	
252	   Phase-specific impulse and IKD peak extension and flexion torque asymmetry indices
253	(AIs) were calculated for each group (BPTB/HT) at both time points (6 months post-ACLR/9
254	months post-ACLR) to assess and monitor the magnitude and direction of injured-limb
255	function relative to the uninjured limb (Jordan et al., 2015). AI was calculated as:
256	
257	AI = ((Uninjured limb ― ACLR limb)/Larger value of the two legs) x 100
258	
259	A positive AI, hence indicated larger value on the uninjured limb, whereas a negative AI
260	indicated a larger value on the injured limb (Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019).
261	
262	
263	Statistical analyses
264	Descriptive statistics are reported as mean±SD. Standardised effect sizes (ES; Cohen’s d) were
265	reported for all comparisons and interpreted as trivial (d < 0.2), small (0.2 ≤ d < 0.5), medium
266	(0.5 ≤ d < 0.8), and large (d ≥ 0.8) (J. Cohen, 1988). Multiple 2 × 2 mixed-model analysis of
267	variance (ANOVA) tests with factors graft type (BPTB/HT) and time (6/9 months post-ACLR)
268	were used to test for differences in inter-limb asymmetry and for differences in the absolute
269	values of independent limbs (ACLR/uninvolved), for each phase of the CMJ (eccentric decel­
270	eration, concentric and landing phases), for IKD knee extensor and flexor strength, and for CMJ
271	height and IKDC scores. Linear regression models were used to determine the amount of
272	variance in ‘change in phase-specific impulse AI’ explained by either ’change in knee extensor
273	AI‘ or ‘change in knee flexor AI’. An alpha level of 0.05 was used for all statistical tests and
274	analyses were performed using IBM SPSS 2016 (v24, IMB Corp, Somers, NY, USA).
275	
276	
277	Results
278	IKDC questionnaire score improved from 6 to 9 months (F = 19.3, p < 0.001, ES = 0.47).
279	No interaction effect (F = 0.71, p = 0.40) or effect of graft type (F = 0.5, p = 0.48) was
280	found with scores increasing in both BPTB (78.2 ± 10.8 to 82.1 ± 11.2) and HT (79.2 ± 8.4
281	to 84.9 ± 8.0) cohorts. While we found no significant change in CMJ height between
282	testing sessions (F = 1.2, p = 0.27) or between graft types (F = 0.08, p = 0.77), an
283	interaction effect was observed (F = 6.93, p = 0.01) indicating that CMJ height decreased
284	from 6 to 9 months in BPTB athletes (28.9 ± 4.9 to 28.3 ± 4.1 cm) but increased in HT
285	athletes (27.4 ± 7.1 to 28.2 ± 6.4 cm). However, ES were trivial to small (0.02–0.25) and
286	represented mean differences in jump height of less than 1.5 cm.
287	
288	
289	Changes in phase-specific impulse AI and isokinetic strength AI from 6 to 9 months
290	post-ACLR
291	An improvement in strength AI was observed in knee extension (F = 18.02, p < 0.001,
292	ES = −0.50) and knee flexion (F= 6.39, p = 0.02, ES = −0.37) from 6 to 9 months post-
293	ACLR. There were significant main effects of graft type on knee extensor strength AI
294	(F= 11.64, p = 0.001) and flexor strength AI (F = 17.94, p < 0.001), BPTB displaying
295	greater extensor AIs (21.24 vs. 9.95%) and lower flexor AIs (1.24 vs. 14.35%).
296	A significant reduction in phase-specific impulse AI was only found within the con­
297	centric phase of the CMJ (F = 24.25, p < 0.001, ES = −0.42). No significant changes (and
298	 6      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.
299	
300	
301	only trivial ES) were identified for eccentric deceleration AI (F = 2.327, p = 0.14,
302	ES = −0.15) and landing AI (F = 0.506, p = 0.48, ES = 0.11). A main effect of graft type
303	on AI was found for the concentric (F = 10.80, p = 0.002) and eccentric deceleration
304	(F = 20.27, p < 0.001) phases of the CMJ, with larger asymmetries present in BPTB
305	athletes. No significant interaction effects (time*graft) on AI were displayed in either IKD
306	assessment (F = 0.002–0.199, p = 0.657–0.969), nor within any phase of the CMJ
307	(F = 0.51–3.24, p = 0.08–0.48).
308	
309	
310	Changes in absolute isokinetic strength and phase-specific impulse of independent
311	ACLR and uninvolved limbs from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR
312	Absolute values of independent limbs (ACLR/uninvolved) at 6- and 9-month testing
313	sessions are displayed in Table 1 with results of the mixed-model ANOVA presented in
314	Table 2.
315	   From 6 to 9 months post-operatively, the ACLR limb displayed increases in extensor
316	and flexor peak torque (F = 17.25–10.66; p < 0.001–0.002) yet uninvolved limb strength
317	did not significantly change. A main effect of graft was observed within peak extensor
318	torque of the ACLR-limb, with greater extensor strength displayed by HT-ACLR than
319	BPTB-ACLR individuals (F = 5.67; p = 0.022). Reductions in eccentric deceleration
320	impulse were apparent in both the ACLR (F = 8.03; p = 0.007) and uninvolved limb
321	(F = 13.41; p = 0.001). A main effect of graft on phase-specific impulse was only observed
322	in the ACLR limb with higher eccentric deceleration impulse in HT (F = 5.63; p = 0.022).
323	A significant reduction in concentric phase impulse occurred within the uninvolved limb
324	(F = 6.92; p = 0.012). Neither limb exhibited changes in landing impulse over time. No
325	interaction effects (time*graft) were found for any isokinetic strength measure, nor in any
326	CMJ phase, for either limb.
327	
328	
329	Relationship between isokinetic strength and impulse asymmetry changes from 6
330	to 9 months post-ACLR
331	There was a weak positive relationship between the change in isokinetic knee extensor
332	strength AI and the change in CMJ eccentric deceleration impulse AI from 6 to 9 months
333	post-ACLR (p= 0.02, r2 = 0.12). No significant relationship was found between the
334	change in isokinetic knee extensor strength AI and the change in either CMJ concentric
335	impulse AI (p = 0.13, r2 = 0.05) or landing impulse AI (p = 0.50, r2 = 0.01) from 6 to 9
336	months post-ACLR, nor between the change in IKD flexor strength AI and the change in
337	impulse AI within any CMJ phase (p = 0.11–0.95, r2 = < 0.01–0.06) during the same
338	period.
339	
340	
341	Discussion and implications
342	Inter-limb asymmetries decreased between 6 and 9 months post-ACLR for CMJ concentric
343	impulse and for peak torque in knee extension and flexion. Changes in peak torque
344	asymmetries were primarily achieved through an increase in ACLR limb strength; however,
345	improvements in concentric impulse asymmetry arose from decrements within the unin­
346	volved limb. Though no significant changes in the eccentric deceleration or landing impulse

398	inter-limb symmetry throughout this later-stage rehabilitation phase did not differ between
399	graft types for any metric. However, BPTB athletes consistently displayed significantly
400	larger CMJ impulse and knee extensor strength asymmetries, but lower knee flexor strength

406	Changes in isokinetic strength AI and phase-specific impulse AI from 6 to 9 months
407	post-ACLR
408	Athletes demonstrated reductions in peak extensor and flexor torque inter-limb asymme­
409	tries from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR (Figure 1(a)). Asymmetry in quadriceps strength has
410	been associated with altered movement patterns in functional tasks (single-legged hopping,
411	landing, walking), heightened osteoarthritic risk and is a further risk factor for re-injury
412	(Grindem et al., 2016; Lewek et al., 2002; Øiestad et al., 2015; Palmieri-Smith & Lepley,
413	2015), whilst strengthening of the knee flexors is believed to decrease the stress placed upon
414	the ACL graft by controlling knee valgus and anterior translation and rotation of the tibia
415	(Bencke et al., 2018; Markolf et al., 2004). Changes in strength AI were predominately
416	achieved through changes in strength of the ACLR limb, as noted in recent literature
417	assessing rehabilitation up to 6 months post-surgery (Harput et al., 2021; Mirkov et al.,
418	2017). Our findings extend upon these studies and suggest that the uninvolved limb may
419	reasonably be used as a control when monitoring changes in muscle strength during later-
420	stage rehabilitation.

Vertical jump impulse deficits persist from six to
nine months after ACL reconstruction

Jill A. E. Costley, Joshua J. Miles, Enda King & Katherine A. J. Daniels

Vertical jump impulse deficits persist from six to nine months
after ACL reconstruction
                           a
Jill A. E. Costley             , Joshua J. Milesa,b, Enda King            a,c
                                                                                and Katherine A. J. Daniels          a,d,e


a
 Sports Medicine Research Department, Sports Surgery Clinic, Dublin, Republic of Ireland; bDepartment for
Health, University of Bath, Bath, UK; cDepartment of Life Sciences, Roehampton University, London, UK;
d
  Queen’s School of Engineering, University of Bristol, Bristol, UK; eDepartment of Sport and Exercise
Sciences, Manchester Metropolitan University, Manchester, UK


    ABSTRACT                                                                               ARTICLE HISTORY
    Later-stage rehabilitation following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)                  Received 1 October 2020
    reconstruction (ACLR) provides a valuable opportunity to target                        Accepted 11 June 2021
    performance deficits before return to sport. This study aimed to:                      KEYWORDS
    (1) evaluate bilateral counter-movement jump (CMJ) phase-specific                      Anterior cruciate ligament
    impulse and isokinetic strength inter-limb asymmetry progression                       reconstruction; isokinetic
    from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR; and (2) examine the extent to which                      strength; IKDC;
    individual changes in strength asymmetry could explain changes in                      rehabilitation; return to sport
    impulse asymmetry. Male athletes (n = 44) with a hamstring tendon
    or bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft were tested 6 and 9
    months post-ACLR. Two-way mixed-model ANOVAs were used to
    identify inter-session and inter-graft differences in CMJ phase-
    specific impulse asymmetries and knee isokinetic flexor and exten­
    sor strength asymmetries, as well as in absolute impulse and
    strength values of independent (ACLR/uninvolved) limbs. Linear
    regression models were used to assess the relationship between
    changes in impulse asymmetry and strength asymmetry.
    Reductions in strength asymmetry arose from improved ACLR-
    limb performance, whereas concentric impulse asymmetry reduced
    consequent to decreased uninvolved-limb performance and
    eccentric deceleration impulses decreased bilaterally. Graft type
    did not modulate findings. Changes in strength asymmetry had
    little or no ability to explain changes in impulse asymmetry.
    Consideration of approaches that may influence persisting deficits
    observed bi-laterally throughout vertical jumping performance
    post-ACLR may enhance rehabilitation practice.



Introduction
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is a common injury in multi-directional field
sports (Moses et al., 2012). Surgical reconstruction of the ACL with either a bone-patellar
tendon-bone (BPTB) or hamstring (semitendinosus/gracilis) tendon (HT) autograft is
the most commonly selected treatment for athletes who wish to return to sport (RTS)
(Mihelic et al., 2011; Evans et al., 2014; Pinczewski et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2015). Following
ACLR, inter-limb deficits in neuromuscular activation, strength and power metrics are
evident as a result of the injury sustained and of graft harvesting (Myer et al., 2006;

CONTACT Jill A. E. Costley          jillcostley@sportssurgeryclinic.com
© 2021 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
 2      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.


Palmieri-Smith et al., 2008; Xergia et al., 2011). Appropriate post-operative rehabilitation
to address functional inter-limb asymmetries is paramount for improving performance
capabilities and reducing re-injury rates (Buckthorpe, 2019; Grindem et al., 2016).
Successful rehabilitation also reduces the risk of further damage to chondral and menis­
cal structures and the onset of associated co-morbidities such as post-traumatic knee
osteoarthritis (Øiestad et al., 2015).
   A widely evaluated parameter of lower-limb function post-ACLR is knee extensor/
flexor muscle strength, assessed using isokinetic dynamometry (IKD) (Grindem et al.,
2016; Undheim et al., 2015). Although inter-limb strength symmetry is associated with
a lower risk of re-injury following ACLR (Grindem et al., 2016), asymmetries in tempo­
rally related metrics (rate of force development, impulse, etc.) frequently prevail beyond
the attainment of a symmetrical strength profile, even after RTS (Menzel et al., 2013;
Jordan et al., 2020). Pre-RTS assessment of neuromuscular ’readiness‘ should, therefore,
also consider the demands of the sport being returned to (Jordan et al., 2015). In multi-
directional field sports, jumping and landing motions are ubiquitous multi-joint actions
and are often characterised by concentric and eccentric demands (Lorenz, 2016; Miles
et al., 2019). Additionally, high eccentric loading upon initial ground contact (<50 ms)
during rapid deceleration is a known mechanism of non-contact ACL rupture
(Krosshaug et al., 2007). For such reasons, the double leg counter-movement jump
(CMJ) is often of interest in RTS assessment (Menzel et al., 2013; Jordan et al., 2020;
Jordan et al., 2015). In particular, the evaluation of phase-specific CMJ impulses,
obtained from the integration of the force-time profile, has enabled the quantification
and characterisation of asymmetry of distinct components of a single movement
(Baumgart et al., 2017; Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019).
   Vertical ground reaction force (GRF) impulse asymmetry has been identified as
a surrogate marker of knee kinetic deficits (moments and work) (Dai et al., 2014) associated
with heightened ACL re-injury risk (Paterno et al., 2010). Although CMJ concentric phase
symmetry has been found to improve with time after surgery (Read et al., 2020), eccentric
properties have displayed persistent deficits (Dai et al., 2020; Miles et al., 2019; Read et al.,
2020), especially following BPTB-ACLR (Miles et al., 2019), and slower recovery (Read
et al., 2020). However, recent evidence suggests that rates of recovery may be influenced by
graft type. For example, Cristiani et al. (2020) reported that inferior extensor strength
symmetry of BPTB-ACLR, relative to HT-ACLR, required up to 24 months post-
operatively to be addressed. Heightened functional performance asymmetries within
BPTB individuals, as assessed by single leg hop distance (SLHD), required only 6 months
post-ACLR (Cristiani et al., 2020). Yet, the SLHD test lacks the sensitivity to detect altered
technical execution (Cormie et al., 2009; King et al., 2019; Kotsifaki et al., 2019) and its
ability to predict successful outcomes following ACLR has been questioned (Davies et al.,
2020). Due to the common eccentric mechanism of ACL injury (Krosshaug et al., 2007), the
enduring deficits in eccentric qualities reported around the time of RTS (Grindem et al.,
2016; Miles et al., 2019; Read et al., 2020) may be of greater concern. Eccentric deficits have
been associated with an increased re-injury risk and may contribute to the high rates of
contralateral injury exhibited in ACLR populations by encouraging preferential use of the
contralateral limb (Miles et al., 2019; Paterno et al., 2010). In addition, only a weak
relationship has been observed between knee isokinetic strength inter-limb asymmetry
and CMJ impulse asymmetry 9 months post-ACLR (Miles et al., 2019), a time often
                                                                     SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        3


associated with RTS (Grindem et al., 2016). Thus, specific consideration of eccentric deficits
may be crucial when determining an athlete’s readiness to RTS; especially within the BPTB-
ACLR population who are reported to display the largest CMJ eccentric deficits, 9 months
post-surgery (Miles et al., 2019).
   Later-stage rehabilitation prior to RTS offers a valuable opportunity to optimise clinically-
related ACLR outcome measures in preparation for the on-field demands of play
(Buckthorpe, 2019; Grindem et al., 2016; Myer et al., 2006). Understanding the progression
of symmetry within key parameters of rehabilitation during this stage may allow persistent
asymmetries to be targeted more precisely, thereby increasing specificity of later-stage
rehabilitative protocols and RTS criteria. Thus, the aims of this study were two-fold: (1)
investigate the presence of systematic changes in CMJ phase-specific impulse and isokinetic
strength asymmetries between 6 and 9 months post-ACLR and whether they are affected by
graft type; and (2) examine the extent to which individual changes in impulse asymmetry can
be explained by changes in strength asymmetry. To assist with interpretations, we further
evaluated absolute values in all assessed strength and impulse variables of the independent
ACLR- and uninvolved-limb to investigate how observed changes in symmetry arose. It was
hypothesised that asymmetries in strength and phase-specific impulse would reduce from 6
to 9 months post-ACLR and that the magnitude of the reduction would not be modulated by
graft type. We expected that only weak relationships would be found between the progression
of strength asymmetries and the progression of CMJ impulse asymmetries, and that this
relationship would be strongest for the concentric phase of the jump.


Methods
Participants
Forty-four 18–35-year-old amateur male multidirectional field sport athletes undergoing
primary ACLR surgery at the Sports Surgery Clinic, Dublin, participated in this study.
Power analysis (G*Power, version 3.1.9.2, Universität Düsseldorf), recruitment proce­
dure, cohort demographics and anthropometric characteristics were as documented
previously (Miles et al., 2019). Participants had stated an intention to return to multi-
directional field sport and had undergone ACLR using either a hamstrings tendon (HT;
semitendinosus and gracilis; n = 22; age 26.1 ± 4.4 years, height 179.4 ± 6.1 cm, body mass
79.8 ± 9.4 kg) or BPTB (n = 22; age 23.4 ± 4.4 years, height 181.8 ± 6.4 cm, body mass
85.2 ± 11.5 kg) autologous ipsilateral graft. Those with previous ACLR, multiple con­
current ligament reconstructions or without an intention to return to multi-directional
field sports were excluded. Participants were predominantly involved in Gaelic football
(39%), hurling (23%), soccer (32%) and rugby (16%). Following ACLR, athletes com­
pleted two testing sessions: the first session at 5–7 months post-surgery (’6-month test’)
and the following at 8–10 months post-surgery (’9-month test’). Mean and standard
deviation (SD) time from surgery to the 6-month test was 6.2 ± 0.4 months (BPTB
6.4 ± 0.4, HT 6.1 ± 0.2) and to the 9-month test was 9.3 ± 0.4 months (BPTB 9.4 ± 0.4, HT
9.1 ± 0.3). At the 6- and 9-month testing session, respectively, the number of participants
that had returned to any level of sport was two and 22, while those who had returned to
their pre-injury level of sport was 0 and 12. The study was approved by the hospital’s
 4      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.


research ethics committee and informed written consent was obtained from participants
before testing. All testing procedures were as reported in Miles et al. (2019).


Testing procedures
Counter-movement jump performance
An identical protocol was used in the testing sessions 6 months and 9 months post-
ACLR, with each session beginning with the measurement of height and body mass.
A standardised warm-up consisting of a two-minute submaximal run at a self-
determined pace and five unloaded squats was subsequently performed and followed
by two maximal familiarisation CMJs. Participants were instructed to jump for maximal
height with lower limbs extended while airborne and hands placed on the iliac crests.
Three maximal CMJs were then performed on two force platforms (BP400600; AMTI,
Massachusetts, USA; 400 × 600 mm) with bilateral vertical ground reaction forces
(vGRF) recorded at 1000 Hz. Participants then completed a clinical assessment protocol
comprising additional jumps and change of direction manoeuvres.

Concentric knee extensor and flexor strength
After laboratory testing, participants undertook a standardised, seated, IKD (Cybex
Humac NORM, CSMI) testing protocol to assess concentric knee flexor and extensor
strength (Undheim et al., 2015). The uninjured limb was tested first. For each limb, the
protocol consisted of three sets of five repetitions (60°/s) interspersed with 60 s rest: one
submaximal warm-up set followed by two maximal-effort sets with verbal encourage­
ment provided throughout. Concentric knee extensor and flexor peak torque was eval­
uated through 100° of range from 0° extension and sampled at 100 Hz. Finally, subjective
knee function was evaluated via the International Knee Documentation Committee
(IKDC) questionnaire (Irrgang et al., 2001).


Data processing
The impulse–momentum relationship was used to calculate vertical velocity of the centre of
mass (COM) at the instant of CMJ take-off (Linthorne, 2001), enabling the determination
of peak CMJ height. Three key phases of the CMJ were then identified using COM vertical
velocity: eccentric deceleration from maximal downwards velocity to zero velocity, con­
centric from zero velocity to take-off, and landing from landing to zero velocity
(Appendix 1) (Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019). The instants of take-off and landing
were identified using a vGRF threshold of 10 N. For each phase, limb-specific impulses were
derived by integration of force–time curves with extraction of impulse parameters facili­
tated by a custom MATLAB script (version 2015a, Mathworks Inc, Massachusetts, USA).
The mean of the three trials was used for all analysis.
   For evaluation of knee extension-flexion strength, a gravity correction was first
applied to IKD outputs. Peak knee extension and flexion torques were then obtained
from the maximal-effort set with the largest maximum knee extension torque and
repetition peak torque coefficient of <0.1. Both GRF impulses and isokinetic torques
were divided by body mass prior to further analysis.
                                                                    SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        5


   Phase-specific impulse and IKD peak extension and flexion torque asymmetry indices
(AIs) were calculated for each group (BPTB/HT) at both time points (6 months post-ACLR/9
months post-ACLR) to assess and monitor the magnitude and direction of injured-limb
function relative to the uninjured limb (Jordan et al., 2015). AI was calculated as:

AI = ((Uninjured limb ― ACLR limb)/Larger value of the two legs) x 100

A positive AI, hence indicated larger value on the uninjured limb, whereas a negative AI
indicated a larger value on the injured limb (Jordan et al., 2015; Miles et al., 2019).


Statistical analyses
Descriptive statistics are reported as mean±SD. Standardised effect sizes (ES; Cohen’s d) were
reported for all comparisons and interpreted as trivial (d < 0.2), small (0.2 ≤ d < 0.5), medium
(0.5 ≤ d < 0.8), and large (d ≥ 0.8) (J. Cohen, 1988). Multiple 2 × 2 mixed-model analysis of
variance (ANOVA) tests with factors graft type (BPTB/HT) and time (6/9 months post-ACLR)
were used to test for differences in inter-limb asymmetry and for differences in the absolute
values of independent limbs (ACLR/uninvolved), for each phase of the CMJ (eccentric decel­
eration, concentric and landing phases), for IKD knee extensor and flexor strength, and for CMJ
height and IKDC scores. Linear regression models were used to determine the amount of
variance in ‘change in phase-specific impulse AI’ explained by either ’change in knee extensor
AI‘ or ‘change in knee flexor AI’. An alpha level of 0.05 was used for all statistical tests and
analyses were performed using IBM SPSS 2016 (v24, IMB Corp, Somers, NY, USA).


Results
IKDC questionnaire score improved from 6 to 9 months (F = 19.3, p < 0.001, ES = 0.47).
No interaction effect (F = 0.71, p = 0.40) or effect of graft type (F = 0.5, p = 0.48) was
found with scores increasing in both BPTB (78.2 ± 10.8 to 82.1 ± 11.2) and HT (79.2 ± 8.4
to 84.9 ± 8.0) cohorts. While we found no significant change in CMJ height between
testing sessions (F = 1.2, p = 0.27) or between graft types (F = 0.08, p = 0.77), an
interaction effect was observed (F = 6.93, p = 0.01) indicating that CMJ height decreased
from 6 to 9 months in BPTB athletes (28.9 ± 4.9 to 28.3 ± 4.1 cm) but increased in HT
athletes (27.4 ± 7.1 to 28.2 ± 6.4 cm). However, ES were trivial to small (0.02–0.25) and
represented mean differences in jump height of less than 1.5 cm.


Changes in phase-specific impulse AI and isokinetic strength AI from 6 to 9 months
post-ACLR
An improvement in strength AI was observed in knee extension (F = 18.02, p < 0.001,
ES = −0.50) and knee flexion (F= 6.39, p = 0.02, ES = −0.37) from 6 to 9 months post-
ACLR. There were significant main effects of graft type on knee extensor strength AI
(F= 11.64, p = 0.001) and flexor strength AI (F = 17.94, p < 0.001), BPTB displaying
greater extensor AIs (21.24 vs. 9.95%) and lower flexor AIs (1.24 vs. 14.35%).
A significant reduction in phase-specific impulse AI was only found within the con­
centric phase of the CMJ (F = 24.25, p < 0.001, ES = −0.42). No significant changes (and
 6      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.


only trivial ES) were identified for eccentric deceleration AI (F = 2.327, p = 0.14,
ES = −0.15) and landing AI (F = 0.506, p = 0.48, ES = 0.11). A main effect of graft type
on AI was found for the concentric (F = 10.80, p = 0.002) and eccentric deceleration
(F = 20.27, p < 0.001) phases of the CMJ, with larger asymmetries present in BPTB
athletes. No significant interaction effects (time*graft) on AI were displayed in either IKD
assessment (F = 0.002–0.199, p = 0.657–0.969), nor within any phase of the CMJ
(F = 0.51–3.24, p = 0.08–0.48).


Changes in absolute isokinetic strength and phase-specific impulse of independent
ACLR and uninvolved limbs from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR
Absolute values of independent limbs (ACLR/uninvolved) at 6- and 9-month testing
sessions are displayed in Table 1 with results of the mixed-model ANOVA presented in
Table 2.
   From 6 to 9 months post-operatively, the ACLR limb displayed increases in extensor
and flexor peak torque (F = 17.25–10.66; p < 0.001–0.002) yet uninvolved limb strength
did not significantly change. A main effect of graft was observed within peak extensor
torque of the ACLR-limb, with greater extensor strength displayed by HT-ACLR than
BPTB-ACLR individuals (F = 5.67; p = 0.022). Reductions in eccentric deceleration
impulse were apparent in both the ACLR (F = 8.03; p = 0.007) and uninvolved limb
(F = 13.41; p = 0.001). A main effect of graft on phase-specific impulse was only observed
in the ACLR limb with higher eccentric deceleration impulse in HT (F = 5.63; p = 0.022).
A significant reduction in concentric phase impulse occurred within the uninvolved limb
(F = 6.92; p = 0.012). Neither limb exhibited changes in landing impulse over time. No
interaction effects (time*graft) were found for any isokinetic strength measure, nor in any
CMJ phase, for either limb.


Relationship between isokinetic strength and impulse asymmetry changes from 6
to 9 months post-ACLR
There was a weak positive relationship between the change in isokinetic knee extensor
strength AI and the change in CMJ eccentric deceleration impulse AI from 6 to 9 months
post-ACLR (p= 0.02, r2 = 0.12). No significant relationship was found between the
change in isokinetic knee extensor strength AI and the change in either CMJ concentric
impulse AI (p = 0.13, r2 = 0.05) or landing impulse AI (p = 0.50, r2 = 0.01) from 6 to 9
months post-ACLR, nor between the change in IKD flexor strength AI and the change in
impulse AI within any CMJ phase (p = 0.11–0.95, r2 = < 0.01–0.06) during the same
period.


Discussion and implications
Inter-limb asymmetries decreased between 6 and 9 months post-ACLR for CMJ concentric
impulse and for peak torque in knee extension and flexion. Changes in peak torque
asymmetries were primarily achieved through an increase in ACLR limb strength; however,
improvements in concentric impulse asymmetry arose from decrements within the unin­
volved limb. Though no significant changes in the eccentric deceleration or landing impulse

asymmetries or jump heights were identified, bilateral reductions in eccentric deceleration
impulse were observed. Changes in knee extensor and flexor strength asymmetry had little
to no ability to explain changes in phase-specific impulse AI. The rate of progression of
inter-limb symmetry throughout this later-stage rehabilitation phase did not differ between
graft types for any metric. However, BPTB athletes consistently displayed significantly
larger CMJ impulse and knee extensor strength asymmetries, but lower knee flexor strength
asymmetries, than HT athletes at both 6 and 9 months post-ACLR. Additionally, absolute
eccentric deceleration impulse and knee extensor strength of the ACLR limb were sig­
nificantly lower in BPTB athletes throughout the investigatory period.


Changes in isokinetic strength AI and phase-specific impulse AI from 6 to 9 months
post-ACLR
Athletes demonstrated reductions in peak extensor and flexor torque inter-limb asymme­
tries from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR (Figure 1(a)). Asymmetry in quadriceps strength has
been associated with altered movement patterns in functional tasks (single-legged hopping,
landing, walking), heightened osteoarthritic risk and is a further risk factor for re-injury
(Grindem et al., 2016; Lewek et al., 2002; Øiestad et al., 2015; Palmieri-Smith & Lepley,
2015), whilst strengthening of the knee flexors is believed to decrease the stress placed upon
the ACL graft by controlling knee valgus and anterior translation and rotation of the tibia
(Bencke et al., 2018; Markolf et al., 2004). Changes in strength AI were predominately
achieved through changes in strength of the ACLR limb, as noted in recent literature
assessing rehabilitation up to 6 months post-surgery (Harput et al., 2021; Mirkov et al.,
2017). Our findings extend upon these studies and suggest that the uninvolved limb may
reasonably be used as a control when monitoring changes in muscle strength during later-
stage rehabilitation.

462	
463	
464	   No significant changes were identified in impulse asymmetries within the eccentric
465	deceleration or landing phases from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR. Persisting deficits in
466	eccentric qualities following ACLR are consistent with previous reports (Read et al.,
467	2020). However, concurrent bilateral reductions in eccentric impulse were observed. Due
468	to the eccentric mechanism associated with many ACL injuries (Krosshaug et al., 2007),
469	the absence of recovery of eccentric function within dynamic movement may contribute
470	to the high rates of re-rupture 11% (Pinczewski et al., 2007) or contralateral rupture
471	especially in BPTB- versus HT-reconstructed individuals with contralateral rupture rates
472	of 5–30% and 2–14%, respectively (Pinczewski et al., 2007; Rousseau et al., 2019;
473	Thompson et al., 2016). Compared to HT-ACLR, ACLR-limb eccentric impulse of the
474	BTPB cohort remained significantly lower throughout later-stage rehabilitation and
475	inter-limb asymmetry remained approximately three-fold greater. Though an emphasis
476	within rehabilitative literature has traditionally been placed upon concentric-based
477	movements (Lepley et al., 2017; Undheim et al., 2015), concentric exercise may fail to
478	provide the required stimuli for complete restoration of neuromuscular function (Lepley
479	et al., 2017). Thus, approaches to negate reductions, and enable improvements, in
480	bilateral eccentric functioning should be considered during later-stage rehabilitation.
481	   The use of the uninvolved limb as a ‘control’ to assess readiness of the ACLR limb
482	post-reconstruction in calculations of inter-limb symmetry is a common approach for
483	monitoring rehabilitation status (Dai et al., 2020). In the absence of pre-injury data, such
484	assessment has been suggested to allow comparisons of the ACLR-limb to ‘uninjured’
485	performance (Dai et al., 2020). However, as our study highlights, measuring asymmetry
486	progression alone may overestimate functional ACLR-limb performance by concealing
487	deleterious uninvolved limb deficits. Though not assessed here, neural and peripheral
488	deficits are argued to ‘crossover’ to the uninvolved limb following ACL rupture and may
489	affect strength and functional performance (Lepley et al., 2017). Detraining effects may
490	also influence both limbs. Thus, utilising the uninvolved limb as a ‘gold standard’
491	benchmark for monitoring ACLR-limb performance and function is not an appropriate
492	strategy to use in isolation, and should be used alongside assessments of independent
493	limbs.
494	
495	
496	Relationship between isokinetic strength and impulse asymmetry changes from 6
497	to 9 months post-ACLR
498	Phase-specific CMJ impulses displayed notably smaller mean changes in asymmetry than
499	IKD knee flexor and extensor strength (Figure 1). The ability of ‘change in knee peak
500	extensor/flexor torque’ to explain ‘change in impulse symmetry’ was also limited, with no
501	significant relationship with concentric or landing phase asymmetry identified and only
502	12% of the variation in eccentric deceleration phase asymmetry explained by the change
503	in knee peak extensor torque (see Appendix 2). The inadequacy of changes in IKD peak
504	torque to predict and monitor deficits in impulse is a finding supported by others
505	(Menzel et al., 2013; Miles et al., 2019; Webster & Hewett, 2019), and may indicate that
506	asymmetries observed in both metrics are relatively distinct entities (Menzel et al., 2013).
507	Jumping performance relies on multi-joint and inter-muscular coordination (Kipp &
508	Kim, 2020) with knee angular velocities of beyond 500°/s (Soest et al., 1985), as opposed
509	to the joint-specific IKD assessment (60°/s) most commonly employed to monitor ACLR
510	 12      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.
511	
512	
513	(Undheim et al., 2015). Following ACLR, changes in spinal-reflex excitability and
514	muscular activation patterns have been reported (He et al., 2020; Pietrosimone et al.,
515	2015), with deficits in neuromuscular control associated with both compensatory move­
516	ment patterns and ACL re-injury risk (Paterno et al., 2010). Deficits of such may prevail
517	beyond the attainment of symmetry in strength indices (Hartigan et al., 2009; Di Stasi
518	et al., 2013) and may hence require an extended duration of rehabilitation, especially
519	those parameterising eccentric properties (Lepley et al., 2017).
520	   There are several limitations to this study. Firstly, GRF integrals cannot directly assess
521	joint loading, although inter-limb deficits in vertical GRF impulse can be used as
522	a surrogate indicator of knee kinetic asymmetries (Dai et al., 2014) associated with ACL
523	re-injury (Paterno et al., 2010). As rehabilitation progresses, the contribution from other
524	joints to movement may increase in an attempt to counteract persisting effects of ACLR
525	(Mueske et al., 2020). Additional evaluation of kinematic and joint moments may, there­
526	fore, heighten the understanding of ACLR rehabilitation beyond GRF kinetics alone.
527	Secondly, post-operative rehabilitation was neither monitored nor closely controlled, ‘pre-
528	injury level’ sporting participation (exposure to dynamic landing tasks) was greater 9
529	months post-surgery (n = 12) than at the 6-month test (n = 0). The mean age of the HT
530	cohort was also greater than that of the BPBT cohort by 2.6 years. These factors may
531	contribute to the variability displayed in several investigated metrics. Although lower
532	variability would be expected in a more tightly controlled cohort of elite athletes (such as
533	the cohorts studied by Jordan et al. (2020) and Read et al. (2020)), the applicability of
534	findings to a broader athletic population may be reduced. To minimise variability,
535	a double leg rather than SL task, was selected to limit any associated confounders such
536	as unilateral postural control, common following ACLR (D. Cohen, et al., 2020; Dai et al.,
537	2020; Mohammadi & Salavati, 2012). However, ACL rupture normally occurs during SL
538	tasks (rapid landing/decelerations) during which athletes are not able to compensate with
539	the contralateral limb (Benjanuvatra et al., 2013). Thus, future work should consider
540	changes in absolute performance, as well as inter-limb asymmetry, of limbs during SL
541	tasks following ACLR and to identify the factors that may influence the measured bilateral
542	regression of the metrics investigated within this study.
543	
544	
545	Conclusion
546	We observed changes in strength asymmetry from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR that were
547	primarily a result of improved ACLR-limb strength. However, improvements in con­
548	centric impulse asymmetry arose from reductions of uninvolved-limb performance.
549	Though eccentric deceleration impulse asymmetry remained unchanged, bilateral reduc­
550	tions in this metric were also evident. The use of the uninvolved limb as a ‘gold standard’
551	benchmark for assessing and monitoring rehabilitation prior to RTS following ACLR
552	may lead to overestimation of functional status of the ACLR-limb by concealing deleter­
553	ious deficits in both concentric and eccentric qualities of the uninvolved limb. Although
554	autograft type did not affect the progression of intra-limb performance over the inves­
555	tigatory time phase, eccentric impulse and quadriceps strength remained consistently
556	lower following BPTB-ACLR compared to HT-ACLR. Consideration of the approaches
557	that may influence the absence of progression in jump-related qualities of both the
558	                                                                      SPORTS BIOMECHANICS         13
559	
560	
561	ACLR- and uninvolved-limb from 6 to 9 months following ACLR may enhance rehabi­
562	litation guidelines and, thus, ACLR outcomes for both autograft types.
563	
564	
565	Perspectives
566	We contribute to the understanding of recovery following ACLR by highlighting that
567	recovery prior to RTS needs to consider both limbs, as well as the capability assessed.
568	Bilateral deficits may be masked, and ACLR-limb functional status overestimated, when
569	using isolated assessments of inter-limb symmetry that utilise post-operative outputs from
570	the uninvolved limb as the ‘benchmark’. In particular, the lack of progression in vertical
571	jump impulse deficits during later-stage rehabilitation and the decrements in uninvolved
572	limb functional performance indicate that more specific, bilateral, interventions and assess­
573	ments may be required to improve outcomes and reduce re-injury rates after ACLR,
574	irrespective of graft type. Nonetheless, BPTB-reconstructed individuals, who consistently
575	displayed lower eccentric impulse and quadriceps strength in the ACLR limb throughout
576	later-stage rehabilitation, may benefit from earlier specification of rehabilitation (<6 months
577	post-operative) to address the temporal discrepancy in recovery times displayed between
578	grafts. This may assist with addressing the higher rates of contralateral rupture observed in
579	this population (Pinczewski et al., 2007; Rousseau et al., 2019; Thompson et al., 2016).

    Although the rate of progression in strength symmetry was not dependent upon
autograft selection in this study, previous findings suggest a heightened recovery rate
of extensor strength symmetry following BPTB than HT-ACLR (Aune et al., 2001;
Cristiani et al., 2020), albeit gradually up to 24 months (Cristiani et al., 2020) post-
operatively. The 3-month observation utilised within our study may, therefore, not be
sufficient to detect differential rates between graft types for measures of strength.
Nonetheless, larger inter-limb extensor and flexor mechanism deficits in respective
BPTB and HT cohorts were observed throughout the investigated rehabilitation period;
as previously reported (Cristiani et al., 2020; Xergia et al., 2011). Morbidity associated
with graft harvesting (Xergia et al., 2011) likely contributes towards this graft differential
response. Thus, a continued focus on strength restoration for both graft types is likely to
be warranted.
    The concentric phase was the only CMJ phase to have a significant decrease in impulse
asymmetry from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR, which occurred in the absence of an
identified improvement in jump height. Previous studies have also reported concentric
impulse asymmetry to display the most consistent improvements over time following
ACLR, in comparison to kinetic asymmetries within other CMJ phases (Jordan et al.,
2020; Read et al., 2020). The reduction in concentric impulse AI from 6 to 9 months post-
ACLR did not differ depending upon graft type (Cristiani et al., 2020). Although Cristiani
et al. (2020) found higher SLHD symmetry in HT-ACLR four months following surgery,

differences between grafts had been negated 6 months post-operatively and is, thus, in
agreement with our findings. However, the improvement in asymmetry as observed
within the current study primarily arose from reductions in ‘uninvolved’ limb perfor­
mance. Given that impulse is the integral of GRF over time, reductions in concentric
impulse may have potential consequences for rapid force generation, limiting sporting
performance upon RTS (Read et al., 2020; Ugrinowitsch et al., 2007).
                                                                 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       11


   No significant changes were identified in impulse asymmetries within the eccentric
deceleration or landing phases from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR. Persisting deficits in
eccentric qualities following ACLR are consistent with previous reports (Read et al.,
2020). However, concurrent bilateral reductions in eccentric impulse were observed. Due
to the eccentric mechanism associated with many ACL injuries (Krosshaug et al., 2007),
the absence of recovery of eccentric function within dynamic movement may contribute
to the high rates of re-rupture 11% (Pinczewski et al., 2007) or contralateral rupture
especially in BPTB- versus HT-reconstructed individuals with contralateral rupture rates
of 5–30% and 2–14%, respectively (Pinczewski et al., 2007; Rousseau et al., 2019;
Thompson et al., 2016). Compared to HT-ACLR, ACLR-limb eccentric impulse of the
BTPB cohort remained significantly lower throughout later-stage rehabilitation and
inter-limb asymmetry remained approximately three-fold greater. Though an emphasis
within rehabilitative literature has traditionally been placed upon concentric-based
movements (Lepley et al., 2017; Undheim et al., 2015), concentric exercise may fail to
provide the required stimuli for complete restoration of neuromuscular function (Lepley
et al., 2017). Thus, approaches to negate reductions, and enable improvements, in
bilateral eccentric functioning should be considered during later-stage rehabilitation.
   The use of the uninvolved limb as a ‘control’ to assess readiness of the ACLR limb
post-reconstruction in calculations of inter-limb symmetry is a common approach for
monitoring rehabilitation status (Dai et al., 2020). In the absence of pre-injury data, such
assessment has been suggested to allow comparisons of the ACLR-limb to ‘uninjured’
performance (Dai et al., 2020). However, as our study highlights, measuring asymmetry
progression alone may overestimate functional ACLR-limb performance by concealing
deleterious uninvolved limb deficits. Though not assessed here, neural and peripheral
deficits are argued to ‘crossover’ to the uninvolved limb following ACL rupture and may
affect strength and functional performance (Lepley et al., 2017). Detraining effects may
also influence both limbs. Thus, utilising the uninvolved limb as a ‘gold standard’
benchmark for monitoring ACLR-limb performance and function is not an appropriate
strategy to use in isolation, and should be used alongside assessments of independent
limbs.


Relationship between isokinetic strength and impulse asymmetry changes from 6
to 9 months post-ACLR
Phase-specific CMJ impulses displayed notably smaller mean changes in asymmetry than
IKD knee flexor and extensor strength (Figure 1). The ability of ‘change in knee peak
extensor/flexor torque’ to explain ‘change in impulse symmetry’ was also limited, with no
significant relationship with concentric or landing phase asymmetry identified and only
12% of the variation in eccentric deceleration phase asymmetry explained by the change
in knee peak extensor torque (see Appendix 2). The inadequacy of changes in IKD peak
torque to predict and monitor deficits in impulse is a finding supported by others
(Menzel et al., 2013; Miles et al., 2019; Webster & Hewett, 2019), and may indicate that
asymmetries observed in both metrics are relatively distinct entities (Menzel et al., 2013).
Jumping performance relies on multi-joint and inter-muscular coordination (Kipp &
Kim, 2020) with knee angular velocities of beyond 500°/s (Soest et al., 1985), as opposed
to the joint-specific IKD assessment (60°/s) most commonly employed to monitor ACLR
 12      J. A. E. COSTLEY ET AL.


(Undheim et al., 2015). Following ACLR, changes in spinal-reflex excitability and
muscular activation patterns have been reported (He et al., 2020; Pietrosimone et al.,
2015), with deficits in neuromuscular control associated with both compensatory move­
ment patterns and ACL re-injury risk (Paterno et al., 2010). Deficits of such may prevail
beyond the attainment of symmetry in strength indices (Hartigan et al., 2009; Di Stasi
et al., 2013) and may hence require an extended duration of rehabilitation, especially
those parameterising eccentric properties (Lepley et al., 2017).
   There are several limitations to this study. Firstly, GRF integrals cannot directly assess
joint loading, although inter-limb deficits in vertical GRF impulse can be used as
a surrogate indicator of knee kinetic asymmetries (Dai et al., 2014) associated with ACL
re-injury (Paterno et al., 2010). As rehabilitation progresses, the contribution from other
joints to movement may increase in an attempt to counteract persisting effects of ACLR
(Mueske et al., 2020). Additional evaluation of kinematic and joint moments may, there­
fore, heighten the understanding of ACLR rehabilitation beyond GRF kinetics alone.
Secondly, post-operative rehabilitation was neither monitored nor closely controlled, ‘pre-
injury level’ sporting participation (exposure to dynamic landing tasks) was greater 9
months post-surgery (n = 12) than at the 6-month test (n = 0). The mean age of the HT
cohort was also greater than that of the BPBT cohort by 2.6 years. These factors may
contribute to the variability displayed in several investigated metrics. Although lower
variability would be expected in a more tightly controlled cohort of elite athletes (such as
the cohorts studied by Jordan et al. (2020) and Read et al. (2020)), the applicability of
findings to a broader athletic population may be reduced. To minimise variability,
a double leg rather than SL task, was selected to limit any associated confounders such
as unilateral postural control, common following ACLR (D. Cohen, et al., 2020; Dai et al.,
2020; Mohammadi & Salavati, 2012). However, ACL rupture normally occurs during SL
tasks (rapid landing/decelerations) during which athletes are not able to compensate with
the contralateral limb (Benjanuvatra et al., 2013). Thus, future work should consider
changes in absolute performance, as well as inter-limb asymmetry, of limbs during SL
tasks following ACLR and to identify the factors that may influence the measured bilateral
regression of the metrics investigated within this study.


Conclusion
We observed changes in strength asymmetry from 6 to 9 months post-ACLR that were
primarily a result of improved ACLR-limb strength. However, improvements in con­
centric impulse asymmetry arose from reductions of uninvolved-limb performance.
Though eccentric deceleration impulse asymmetry remained unchanged, bilateral reduc­
tions in this metric were also evident. The use of the uninvolved limb as a ‘gold standard’
benchmark for assessing and monitoring rehabilitation prior to RTS following ACLR
may lead to overestimation of functional status of the ACLR-limb by concealing deleter­
ious deficits in both concentric and eccentric qualities of the uninvolved limb. Although
autograft type did not affect the progression of intra-limb performance over the inves­
tigatory time phase, eccentric impulse and quadriceps strength remained consistently
lower following BPTB-ACLR compared to HT-ACLR. Consideration of the approaches
that may influence the absence of progression in jump-related qualities of both the
                                                                      SPORTS BIOMECHANICS         13


ACLR- and uninvolved-limb from 6 to 9 months following ACLR may enhance rehabi­
litation guidelines and, thus, ACLR outcomes for both autograft types.


Perspectives
We contribute to the understanding of recovery following ACLR by highlighting that
recovery prior to RTS needs to consider both limbs, as well as the capability assessed.
Bilateral deficits may be masked, and ACLR-limb functional status overestimated, when
using isolated assessments of inter-limb symmetry that utilise post-operative outputs from
the uninvolved limb as the ‘benchmark’. In particular, the lack of progression in vertical
jump impulse deficits during later-stage rehabilitation and the decrements in uninvolved
limb functional performance indicate that more specific, bilateral, interventions and assess­
ments may be required to improve outcomes and reduce re-injury rates after ACLR,
irrespective of graft type. Nonetheless, BPTB-reconstructed individuals, who consistently
displayed lower eccentric impulse and quadriceps strength in the ACLR limb throughout
later-stage rehabilitation, may benefit from earlier specification of rehabilitation (<6 months
post-operative) to address the temporal discrepancy in recovery times displayed between
grafts. This may assist with addressing the higher rates of contralateral rupture observed in
this population (Pinczewski et al., 2007; Rousseau et al., 2019; Thompson et al., 2016).
